newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka parties show their colours on May Day.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka parties show their colours on May Day.

text.p: Thousands of Sri Lankan workers and political activists marched in Colombo and other towns on Thursday in a show of solidarity on May Day, demanding higher wages and an end to the country's war with separatist rebels.

At least 10 May Day rallies were held around the country, most of them with a festive air in which smiling trade unionists danced to music while gaily decorated floats illustrated worker concerns such as unemployment and the high price of bread.

Security was tight in the capital Colombo where the ruling People's Alliance (PA) held its May Day meeting. Police body-searched an estimated 100,000 people who attended the meeting at the sprawling Town Hall grounds in central Colombo.
Four years ago to the day, former president Ranasinghe Premadasa was killed by a suicide bomber during a May Day rally by the then-ruling United National Party (UNP).

The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), who are fighting for an independent homeland for minority ethnic Tamils in predominantly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east, are suspected of having carried out the assassination. They have not claimed responsibility.
The People's Alliance, fresh from a landslide victory at last March's local government polls, drew supporters from all parts of the island to its rally.

PA supporters carried banners and shouted slogans demanding that political parties shed their narrow differences and work together to end the ethnic war, which the government says has claimed more than 50,000 lives.
The PA, which came to power in 1994 after 17 years of UNP rule, says it has achieved much in this area.

"During the past 32 months, we have scored great victories not only on the battlefronts in the north and east, but also in every sector of the economy," President Chandrika Kumaratunga said in a May Day message.

"As a result of restoration of stability in the country, foreign investors are coming in and many schemes are now under implementation for the improvement of the economic conditions of workers," she said.
The UNP this year held its rally in Hatton, 90 km (56 miles) east of Colombo, in a bid to woo thousands of tea plantation workers in that region.
More than 25,000 people participated in the afternoon rally, participants said.
"The UNP has developed close ties with plantation workers and we decided to hold the rally in that area this time," UNP parliament deputy Sarath Amunugama said.

Amunugama said the UNP, which won handsomely on the plantations at the recent local polls, announced a special package for plantation labourers in a bid to woo them away from their traditional Ceylon Workers Congress (CWC) support base.
The leftwing Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (People's Liberation Front), also held its May Day rally in Colombo.

The JVP, which has carried out two abortive insurgencies in the past 15 years, vowed to remain in mainstream politics after winning 101 seats in the local polls and effectively becoming Sri Lanka's third major political force behind the PA and the UNP, speakers at its meeting said.
